nodes.label: Employee and User Separation (feature document)
nodes.rationale: Running decision document. Topic 10 of the signatory document settled that employees and users become two separate tables; this document works out the design, one topic at a time, recording problem, decision and whether it is still open.

nodes.label: employee table
nodes.rationale: One row per person in the office whether or not they log in. Holds name, position_title, position_short_form, org_unit_fk, birth_date, sex, civil_status, tenure_status, employment_status. Facts about the person live here because a person has one name whether or not they have an account.

nodes.label: user table (login only)
nodes.rationale: Holds only sign-in facts: username, password_hash, role_fk, account_status, must_change_password, failed_login_attempts, locked_until, last_login_at. Name fields were removed so no column is meaningful only for part of the office.

nodes.label: employee_history table (versions of a person)
nodes.rationale: One row per version of a person's name, position title and short form, with valid_from/valid_until. Documents point at a version rather than at the person, so a marriage or a promotion cannot silently rewrite paperwork already filed. employee keeps a current copy so an ordinary lookup stays one read. Its employee_fk cascades on delete, the opposite of every other key here, because restrict would have made every employee undeletable the moment they got their first version; the protection arrives later from the document side.

nodes.label: employee_history_correction log
nodes.rationale: Records which version, which field, old and new value, who corrected it and when. Built because writing over a version corrects every document using it at once, which would otherwise leave no trace. Deliberately shown on no screen for now, since the log fills up from the day it is built either way and a screen built later still shows every repair back to the first.

nodes.label: user.employee_fk — required link
nodes.rationale: The link lives on user, not on employee, because a login always belongs to a person while most people have no login. It is NOT NULL so no screen showing a name needs a branch for an account with no person, and the database rather than application code enforces it. Confirmed by the user that every account in this office belongs to a real human, with no automated jobs.

nodes.label: One employee, one login (unique employee_fk)
nodes.rationale: Enforced by user_employee_fk_unique. Two accounts for one human would make 'who changed this record?' unanswerable. Different permissions are handled by changing the role, not by a second account. Super-admin handover therefore creates a new account rather than passing a password down, which is the office habit that had to change.

nodes.label: role_fk stays on user, not employee
nodes.rationale: 'Role' means two things: role in the office (position_title, on employee) and role in the app (a permission bundle). Keeping role_fk beside username and password means it only exists where it means something, instead of being empty for most of the office and needing a has-a-login check everywhere, a check that is easy to forget.

nodes.label: account_status
nodes.rationale: Renamed from status so that no word is reused for two different ideas across the two tables. Values active, inactive, locked.

nodes.label: employment_status (active / separated)
nodes.rationale: Kept at two values on purpose. Recording why somebody left — retirement, resignation, end of contract, dismissal — starts to overlap with a personnel system, which this project is not.

nodes.label: tenure_status (seven CSC categories)
nodes.rationale: permanent, temporary, casual, coterminous, contractual, cos, job_order. COS and Job Order are listed apart because those people are not government employees under CSC rules. substitute was excluded because the office never fills a post while its holder is on long leave; coterminous is tied to a term or project, not to a person's absence. Required, because the office hires a person into a named post — COS and JO staff hold no plantilla item but still have a designation.

nodes.label: civil_status
nodes.rationale: Optional. Named distinctly from employment_status because 'separated' is the ordinary word both for leaving a job and for a marriage arrangement, and keeping the column names apart is what prevents the confusion.

nodes.label: Duplicate-person check
nodes.rationale: An exact match refuses the save; a possible match warns and lets it through once the admin answers, because a possible match is genuinely ambiguous and the system should inform rather than stand in the way. Written once in duplicate-check.ts and run both live in the dialog and again in the server actions, which cannot be bypassed. Editing runs the same check, excluding the record being edited, and is skipped when name and birthday are untouched so two people sharing a birthday are not re-asked on every save.

nodes.label: Birth date as the identity anchor
nodes.rationale: A birth date never changes, is the same for a man or a woman, and survives marriage, so it replaces an earlier sex-dependent surname branch the user had built elsewhere — one mistyped sex field made that check behave differently, silently. The form requires it while the column stays nullable, which keeps the 'one record has no birth date' rule alive rather than dead code.

nodes.label: Bring this person back (reinstate)
nodes.rationale: An exact match on somebody marked as no longer employed offers reinstatement inside the form rather than only refusing, because a refusal with no way forward is the moment somebody changes a spelling to force the save through — creating the duplicate the check exists to prevent. It also applies the typed position, section, tenure and civil status, since people rarely return to the same job, and names field-by-field what will change.

nodes.label: Two admin pages: Employees and Users
nodes.rationale: One combined dialog would have asked for fourteen things including a password, the two lists are different sizes so account columns would sit empty for most rows, and the two jobs differ — keeping the staff list current is clerical, creating a login decides who may do what. Accepted cost: hiring somebody who needs a login means visiting two places.

nodes.label: admin:view_employees and admin:manage_employees
nodes.rationale: A new employees submodule under admin in PERMISSION_DEFS, so a clerk can keep the staff list current without also being able to create accounts and assign roles. The Users page still lists employees without needing view_employees, because the key controls opening the page, not reading names elsewhere.

nodes.label: Sign-in refuses anyone no longer employed
nodes.rationale: Option C of three, in the user's words: why would we let a person log in if that person is no longer working here. It cannot be forgotten, whereas option B — switching the account off at the same moment — still left a gap, since an admin could switch it back on without touching the employment record. Accepted cost paid in full: the Users page shows a 'Person has left' badge and disables the Active switch so no row reads plain Active for an account that does not work.

nodes.label: endSessionsForEmployee helper
nodes.rationale: Deletes that person's session rows so an open session stops at the next request rather than at its eight-hour expiry. Called from both separate and update, because the editor was a second way in that would otherwise have left the person signed in.

nodes.label: validateSessionToken joins employee
nodes.rationale: An inner join, since user.employee_fk cannot be null. A session whose employee is not active is deleted and treated as no session, rather than merely refused, so the row does not sit until expiry. SessionUser carries a nested employee object rather than a flattened one so it stays visible which table each field came from, and birth date, sex and civil status never leave the server.

nodes.label: position_short_form
nodes.rationale: What is actually printed in the small boxes of the paper forms, for example AO-I/Supply Officer. Nullable because no rule worth trusting turns a full title into an abbreviation, nobody in the system has one yet, and a NOT NULL column would have made the backfill impossible and blocked an admin from correcting a birthday until they had invented one. The document that prints a short form must refuse to print rather than print a blank line.

nodes.label: backfill-employee-history script (2000-01-01)
nodes.rationale: Safe to run twice; skips anybody who already has a version. Every backfilled version starts 2000-01-01, not as a claim that anybody was employed then, but because paper is always typed in after it was signed — a version starting on the day the script ran would leave last week's slip finding nobody. The honest-looking alternative, each person's own created_at, would have broken ordinary back-dated entry from the first day.

nodes.label: valid_until is inclusive; changes take effect today
nodes.rationale: valid_until is the last day the version was still correct. So a change closes the old version yesterday and opens the new one today, or both would be valid today and a document filed today would match one person twice. Separation closes the open version today, because today was still a working day. Two same-day exceptions: a version begun today is corrected in place, and a version closed earlier today is reopened on same-day reinstatement — the second was a bug found in a browser test, not foresight. No typed effective-date field, because two new fields would have to be explained and a mistyped date creates a person who cannot be picked on documents they really signed.

nodes.label: Three doors: edit, add change, correct entry
nodes.rationale: Proposed by the user and it replaced a design that asked a question at save time. The button somebody pressed already says which case it is, so nothing has to be inferred, nothing interrupts a save, and the edit dialog goes back to doing one job. Edit writes over the open version, Add name or position change closes it and opens a new one, and the history sheet corrects one closed version at a time. Known cost kept deliberately: a document reads whichever version covers its own date, so a misspelling on a closed version survives until somebody corrects that version too.

nodes.label: Name and position history sheet
nodes.rationale: A shadcn-svelte sheet opened from the row menu beside Edit, one card per entry newest first, fetched on open rather than with the page because almost nobody opens it. Named by the user over Name history, Change history, Employee history, Service Record and Record of name and position, on the rule that the words must be understandable to anybody without explanation. A row in employee_history is a 'version' in code and an 'entry' on screen.

nodes.label: employee-history.ts — the single write path
nodes.rationale: The only place either employee or employee_history is written, holding createEmployee, updateEmployee, separateEmployee, reinstateEmployee, addEmployeeVersion and correctEmployeeVersion, each entirely inside one db.transaction. This one discipline is what stops the current copy on employee drifting out of step with the open history row, which would make a printed document disagree with the Employees page with no way to tell which was right.

nodes.label: countDocumentsUsingVersions — a stub written to be replaced
nodes.rationale: Returns zero today because no document table exists, and whoever builds the first document naming a signatory must come back to it. The warning still shows at zero rather than hiding, because silence would read as 'nothing to think about here' when the choice still matters, and because back-dated entry means a misspelled version left open still covers earlier dates.

nodes.label: create-admin.ts bootstrap
nodes.rationale: Because user.employee_fk is required it must insert the employee row first and the login second, both in one transaction so a taken username does not leave an orphan employee behind when the prompt retries.

nodes.label: The bootstrap script invents a person who does not exist
nodes.rationale: Open topic. The script writes Admin User / System Administrator / Permanent with no birth date, which contradicts the whole argument for requiring the link — the first login names a made-up person, and a fake row sits in the Employees list looking like staff with nothing forcing anybody to fix it. Decided: the script asks instead of inventing, since it already asks for a username. Still open: exactly which fields it asks for, and whether birth_date should become a required column.

nodes.label: sync-permissions super-admin backfill step
nodes.rationale: Added after the employee keys exposed the gap: the super-admin role is frozen, so a key it does not already hold cannot be granted through the interface at all, and re-normalizing does not help because nothing implies manage_employees — implication only runs upward. Finds the role by admin:manage_roles rather than by name, inserts what is missing in one transaction, names what it added, and skips with a message on a fresh database. Staff keys are deliberately excluded.

nodes.label: drizzle-kit push is unsafe on this project
nodes.rationale: Its way of adding a NOT NULL rule to a MySQL column is to TRUNCATE the table first, and with --force it attempted exactly that on employee. The data survived only because user holds a foreign key onto employee and MySQL refused. Schema changes are applied as plain SQL instead.

nodes.label: EMS is not a personnel system
nodes.rationale: The limit the user set and repeated: follow CSC conventions where they exist so fields feel familiar, but leave records, payroll and service records out. It is what excluded reasons for leaving, a history of when somebody left and returned, and an employee number, since the plantilla item only applies to regular employees and COS and JO staff have none.
